Hey all,
I have been dealing with a very strange situation that I really don't know how to explain it, hoping I could borrow some brain power from here.

The problem is that I have a very simple model which I try to take sample from a multivariate normal with specified mean and cov. However, the cov has a lots of zero elements in it and I'm hoping following the MCMC the simulated variables also keep those zero and near zero values in their cov.

So I compared the simulated outcomes for the same model, data and initial conditions once by compiling it and once with MCMCSuite. The difference is unbelievable. The one that is compiled is very unstable and it's doing much worse in simulating cov s (in upper diagonal matrix) in order of couple of 1000 whereas the MCMCSuite is much closer to zero.

Any thoughts or ideas ?

You can find the code and the outcomes here: http://rpubs.com/Para2x/464195

Thanks so much for raising this concern, Hamze.  The short story, I'm pleased to say, is there's no discrepancy between the result from runMCMC() and MCMCsuite().

The very short reason for what you observed, is a slight difference in handling of (the interplay between) burnin, and thinning, in runMCMC() as compared to MCMCsuite().  I'll also mention that NIMBLE gives an informative message along these lines, when you use runMCMC(), and include *both* a non-zero burnin, and thinning interval > 1.  This message, which was suppressed in the Rpubs document you published, looks like:

samples.list <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, niter = 5e6, nburnin=1e3, nchains = 2, thin=500)
## runMCMC's handling of nburnin changed in nimble version 0.6-11. Previously, nburnin samples were discarded *post-thinning*.  Now nburnin samples are discarded *pre-thinning*.  The number of samples returned will be floor((niter-nburnin)/thin).

If you read this carefully, and/or the documentation for runMCMC() and MCMCsuite() which explains the same thing, then here's the difference:

runMCMC() does burnin *pre-thinning*, so in your case, the number of samples being recorded was:
floor(niter-nburnin)/thin) = floor((5000000 - 1000) / 500) = 9998

Note that in your Rpubs document, MCMCsuite was only being run for 2e6 MCMC iterations, different from the run for runMCMC(),

MCMCsuite() uses older behaviour, where burnin is done *post-thinning*, so the number of samples being recorded was:
floor(niter / thin) - nburnin = floor(2000000 / 500) - 1000 = 4000 - 1000 = 3000

At the end of the day, these differences in the number of samples being executed, and recorded, was giving rise to the discrepancy you noticed.

I've gone ahead and modified your code slightly, just to demonstrate the agreement.  Please look carefully at the comments included, to see the changes I've made (using set.seed(), changing to 1 chain only, executing the same number of samples for each, removing the thinning, and perhaps others).

Thanks again for posting this, and keep in touch with any further questions.

Cheers,
Daniel
for the NIMBLE development team

messages.subject: bugs in NIMBLE affecting (1) WAIC from multiple chains and (2) certain MCMC samplers for Bayesian nonparametric models
messages.subject_clean: bugs in NIMBLE affecting (1) WAIC from multiple chains and (2) certain MCMC samplers for Bayesian nonparametric models
messages.body_plain:
Dear nimble-users group members:

We've recently discovered a couple numerical errors in NIMBLE algorithms
that are fixed in the recently released NIMBLE version 0.7.0.

1) The first bug caused incorrect calculation of WAIC when calculated
from multiple MCMC chains for models with any non-scalar monitored
variables. Note that WAIC calculated from a single chain was not
affected by this bug.

2) The second bug caused incorrect MCMC updating for Bayesian
nonparametric models using the dCRP distribution in cases with the
following conjugacies between the base measure and the mixture kernel:

- dgamma base measure, dnorm kernel (mixing over the precision)
- dgamma base measure, dinvgamma kernel
- dbeta base measure, dbinom kernel
- dbeta base measure, dnegbin kernel
- ddirch base measure, dmulti kernel

Note that other conjugate situations, in particular the dnorm base
measure with dnorm kernel, as well as non-conjugate settings were not
affected by this bug.

We apologize for the errors and strongly encourage anyone who has used
WAIC in the fashion indicated above or used MCMC sampling on a BNP
model with the distributions indicated above to redo their
calculations using the updated 0.7.0 version of NIMBLE.

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team

Hi all,

I am trying to specify a CAR model for segment occupancy (spatially arranged subsamples) within sample units (grid cells) where the number of segments/cell is variable. The relevant code looks like this:

  alpha1[i,1:nsegs[i]] ~ dcar_normal(adj[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]], weights[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]],num[i,1:nsegs[i]], tau1,zero_mean=1)
  weights[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]] <- 1
  # some derivations
  thetahat[i]<-mean(theta[i,1:nsegs[i]])
  meanUse[i]<- mean(u[i,1:nsegs[i]])

This means that sum_neighbors is a dynamic index (and "nsegs"). When I included sum_neighbors in constants, I got an error message:

Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames,  :
  getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse: dynamic indexing of constants is not allowed in sum_neighbors[i]. Try adding the dynamically-indexed constant as data instead (using the data argument of nimbleModel).

As advised, I instead entered it into the model as data. Then I got an error suggesting that sum_neighbors needs to be included in constants!

Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames,  :
  R function ':' has arguments that cannot be evaluated; either the function must be a nimbleFunction or values for the following inputs must be specified as constants in the model: .USED_IN_INDEX(i),.sum_neighbors_unknownIndex_sum_neighbors_oBi_cB_context2[.DYN_INDEXED(i)].

That seems like I am between a rock and a hard place, except for the suggestion to define a nimbleFunction. So I gave that a try, something like this:

CAR_prior <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(adj = double(2), sum_neighbors = double(1),num=double(2),nsegs=double(1),
     tau1=double(0)) { # type declarations
  prior ~ dcar_normal(adj[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]], weights[i,1:sum_neighbors[i]],
    num[i,1:nsegs[i]], tau1,zero_mean=1) # Site level random effects
        return(prior)
        returnType(double(2))  # return type declaration
    } )
....
meanFunc <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(X = double(1),nsegs=double(1),i=double(0)) { # type declarations
  mn <- mean(X[i,1:nsegs[i]])
        return(mn)
        returnType(double(0))  # return type declaration
    } )
....
  alpha1[i,1:nsegs[i]] <- CAR_prior(adj,sum_neighbors,num,nsegs,tau1)
  # some derivations
   thetahat[i]<-meanFunc(theta[i,1:nsegs[i]],nsegs)
  meanUse[i]<- meanFunc(u[i,1:nsegs[i]],nsegs,i=i)

But there were a few issues. First, specifying the function produced a warning about an R function (presumable it is colon operator again):

Warning message:
Detected possible use of R functions in nimbleFunction run code. For this nimbleFunction to compile, these objects must be defined as nimbleFunctions, nimbleFunctionLists, or nimbleLists: ~.

And then when I tried to use the functions anyway, I still got the Error about the R function arguments that can't be evaluated, this time apparently in refence to "nsegs".

There may be deeper issues with my model, but I guess my question for now is this:
Is it possible to use a colon indexing operator when the upper limit specifies a dynamic index (in my call to dcar_normal)?
Is it the colon itself that must be defined as a nimbleFunction?

Thanks,
Glenn

Glenn, thanks so much for your use and interest in NIMBLE, in particular your use of the CAR spatial models.  Let's get this figured out.

Definitely no need to define the colon (" : ") operator as a nimbleFunction, but good on you for considering that.

I feel like what you're trying to do should work fine.  To be clear, I don't believe that in your model sum_neighbors (nor nsegs) is dynamically indexed.  That would imply that the *indexing used for sum_neighbors[]* (same goes for nsegs), itself, is a dynamically-valued node in the model.  In this case, in your model, that index is "i", which I'm guessing is a loop-index (e.g. for(i in 1:N), { .... sum_neighbors[i] .... }.  In the dynamically indexed case, it would rather appear as: i ~ dSomeDistribution(...)

Again, I'm guessing that your use of the index "i" is not a dynamic index, and thus sum_neighbors (nor nsegs) is not dynamically indexed in your model, and therefore you should be fine providing both sum_neighbors and nsegs in as "constants" to the model, as you tried.  So like I said at the beginning, I think what you're trying to do should work fine.

All that said, I can't actually see what's going on, with just the minimal code snippets you provided.  I'm not asking you to share your full model on this public list, nor to share it directly with me.  But if you want us to take a look, we'll need some sort of reproducible example of the problem you're having, so we can figure it out.

Hope this helps!  Keep in touch.

Daniel

Thanks for the quick replies - I have attached an example (which I am not entirely sure is correct). And apologies in advance for the following long post. But I've been trying to do some additional sleuthing, and try here to explain what I have found (or not).

The one piece I’m not sure I mentioned is that some of the cells have only a single segment, so no neighborhood can be defined for those cells. So I used double indexing accounting like Daniel described here (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/hJejjex5C_4 ), where I tried to define a CAR prior for alpha1 in the cases where there were >1 segments, and set alpha1==0 otherwise. That seems to be a problem, because when I drop out that complication and make sure all cells have >2 segments (example also included), then the dynamic indexing error goes away (with nsegs and sum_neighbors included in constants rather than data; including them in data still generates the error about R function arguments than can't be evaluated). However, I did still get a bunch of warnings about NaNs that are produced when I run "nimMC$run(1)", and also another, different error, at the compilation step (of the model).

Cnim <- compileNimble(nim)
Error: Failed to create the shared library

Not sure what is the issue with the NaNs produced, but based on this post (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/a693revKUMM), I thought there might be a type mismatch problem in the compilation. It looks there might be an issue with weights, and indeed, supplying weights as constants eliminated that compilation error. However, there is still the problem with the NaNs, and also at the second compilation step, there is an additional error (sometimes)

CnimMC <- compileNimble(nimMC,project=nim)
Error in `*tmp*`[[jj]] :
  attempt to select less than one element in integerOneIndex

I wasn't able to figure out anything from looking at the compiler output, but curiously, when I just simply tried it again a second time (just repeated "CnimMC <- compileNimble(nimMC,project=nim)"), it did not produce the error (but seemed to compile suspiciously quickly). And it clearly is not correct, because a call to runMCMC failed. Calling the uncompiled mcmc object didn't fail to run, but predictably produced the same NaN warnings.

All that trial and error above was for the case where all cells have >2 segments. I suspect I might have a silly error somewhere and just can't seem to see it. But I also don't have a lot of experience with spatial models and so am not sure if I am trying to do something ill-advised.

Regarding the scenario where some cells do have only a single segment, there may be a few other issues.

First, when nsegs[i] evaluates to 1, then my model has, in two places, index ranges that evaluate to something like "for(seg in 1:1), or mean(theta[i,1:1]). I'm not sure if such indexing is allowed.

Second, of course, if number of segments is generated randomly (as in a simulation), than the model is completely inappropriate if by chance all of the cells have >1 segment. In that case, I think it would be easy to have a switch to use another model. What is less clear to me is if the model should work if only one cell has a single segment. I think maybe it would fail in that case as well (at the compilations step) because then the index vector for the cells than have only 1 segment (no_neighbors) would be of length 1, and the attempt to index it with no_neighbors[ind] would be problematic (a type mismatch again). If so, I could probably again write a clever switch to deal with such a case. But at this point, I can't get past the dynamic indexing issue.

Thanks,

Glenn

Glenn, I've made a lot of progress with your model, and fixed a number of problems.  I'll encourage you to carefully look through the attached script (sandbox_DT.R), with particular attention to the comments I've added which begin with "DT: ...", where I've added some helpful or explanatory comments.

That said, I wasn't able to completely fix the first model, as there's a problem with your generation of the adjacency matrix, and I'm not sure what the intent of your code was exactly, but I am sure it's not doing what you're intended.  Specifically, in the case where nsegs = 2, which happens in your example when ind=15, the function you wrote getAdjMatrix() to generate the adj matrix, I don't believe it's functioning correctly in that case of nsegs = 2.

In that case, then loop for (i in 2:(nsegs[j] - 1)) { ends up doing some "backwards indexing", where the loop indexing constant i take the value of 2, then decrements to take the value of 1.  In this situation, as written, that line of the adjacency matrix (adj[15, ]) ends up having  a "0" in the first position, that is, adj[15, 1] = 0, which cannot be as intended, as it suggests that cell number 15 is a neighbor with cell number 0, which doesn't exist.

This then leads to a new problem in the use of the dcar_normal() distribution, since it has issues with this 0.

That said, I fixed a lot of other problems (in the attached script), so many so that there's a reasonable (well, at least non-zero) chance that if you fix up this issue with the generation of the adj matrix (in the function getAdjMatrix() ), then the first example in this script might just work.

The big issue I'll mention, for you, and for anyone else reading this, was that the BUGS modelling language is *declarative*, that is, every line, or each time a line in a for loop is executed, should declare a *new node*, and not try to define any sort of "intermediate temporary variable".  This was causing a problem (previously) in your lines of model code that looked like:

for(ind in ....) {
    i <- .....
    alpha1[ .... various uses of the i variable ...]
}

Further, interestingly, I was not able to re-create the compilation issue that you had in the second example.  It compiled fine for me.  That said, I don't believe the *model* in the second example was fully well-formed, since model$calculate() returned NA, which generally indicates a problem of some sort.  But I figured at least starting with correcting all the things I've pointed out, will be a good start in updating the second model, as well.

There's a good place to start.  Please keep in touch if you still have issues, once you fix up the adj matrix, and the other things I've pointed out in the attached script.

Cheers!
Daniel

Dear users,

If you have a model with many nodes, you may encounter a mysterious bug in nimble 0.7.0.  You might see a message like "There an unknown problem looking for variables..." [sic] and/or a message about a protect stack overflow.

We have a branch on GitHub that fixes this bug.  To install from this branch, you will need package devtools installed.  Use the following code:

library(devtools)
install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "avoid-protect-stack-overflow", subdir = "packages/nimble")

Thanks to the users who let us know about this.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hey,
I am fitting another event time model with a large dataset (99184 rows) that has routinely crashed R with no error messages. I truncated the data (70 rows) to fewer years to exactly match an analysis done years ago and finally received some error messages. I am recreating this analysis, eventually with a decade of new data.  Consequently, I know this model works and that it can be run with 2009 computers using winbugs.

The model is structured to be expanded into a spatial model, so looks a bit weird, but is ultimately an intercept model with a single parameter beta0.

modelcode = nimbleCode({
  beta0 ~ dflat()
  for (i in 1:N) {
    for (j in (runsum[i]+1):runsum[i+1]) {
      for (k in 1:agem[j]) {
        gamma[j,k]<-(beta0)
        dayhaz[j,k] <- exp(gamma[j,k])
      } #k
      icumhaz[j]<-sum(dayhaz[j,1:agem[j]])
      p[j] <-1-exp(-icumhaz[j])
      pos[j] ~ dbern(p[j])
    } #j
  } #i
})#end model

The model compiles, mcmc runs, then poof error message appears or else R just crashes.

The error messages I've received have been on both the nimble/R side and with a C++ namespace error.

(1) When the model was run using the large dataset using nimbleMCMC with 200000 iterations, I received a nimble/R error:

Error in eval(call(".Call", nimbleUserNamespace$sessionSpecificDll$matrix2VecNim
Arr,  :
  long vectors not supported yet: memory.c:3451

(2) When this same model was run using subsetted data with nimbleMCMC with 100000 iterations, I received a c++ error that then crashed R:

terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::bad_array_new_length'
  what():  std::bad_array_new_length
Aborted (core dumped)

Not sure what to do these errors, or what they mean exactly. Googling suggests that given the large data, perhaps I'm exceeding R limits with respect to matrix size. But the namespace error is perhaps the actual bug? Since this is the least complex model we are planning to use, it's a bit troublesome to have a possible size limit problem.

Thanks for any help you could provide!

messages.body_plain:
Dear nimble-users,

Thanks for Alison for following up with me off-list with her example.  Here is a summary for interested readers of the situation:

The requested samples were > 75Gb.  Although it was being run on a machine with more memory than that, still it seems to be above R's memory limitations.  There is material online about changing R's memory limits.

We were able to make the model faster to build and probably to run by removing dayhaz and replacing icumhaz with icumhaz[j] <- sum(exp(gamma[j, 1:agem[j]])).  We left gamma there as a placeholder for a more complicated model component.  It would also be possible to remove icumhaz[j] and caculate p[j] in a single expression.  In other situations, one can remove large intermediate variables from model code by writing user-defined functions as nimbleFunctions.

We discourage an unnecessary for loop like the loop for i in this case.  Other software does not generate an error in such cases.

The error reported involving matrix2VecNim can only occur when using WAIC=TRUE with multiple chains.  If that were the only issue, it could be avoided by WAIC = FALSE or using only one chain.  However, it seems to go hand-in-hand with requesting huge MCMC samples.  We don't have a case where this error is triggered except in this context of overall too much memory use, although in theory it could be possible.

-Perry

messages.subject: specifying inits in runMCMC
messages.body_plain:
Too many posts from me in the last few days, but one more question.

Has there been a change recently in how the function runMCMC uses provided initial values?
If I compile and run a model once, then use Cnim$setData(NewData) to insert new data into the model, it appears that "runMCMC" does not actually use the inits that are provided in the call to that function. It generates warnings about certain nodes where logProb is -Inf.
Take a simple site occupancy model as an example:

model <- nimbleCode({
    psi ~ dunif(0,1)
    p ~ dunif(0,1)
    for(i in 1:ncells){
        z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
        pz[i] <- p*z[i]
        y[i]~dbin(pz[i],noccs)
    }
})

What seems to be happening is that instead of using the inits for z provided to runMCMC to fit the second data set, it uses as inits the final values in the model from the previous model fitting (the documentation says this is the case if inits are not provided to runMCMC).The result is that in some cases z[i]==0 and y[i]>0, which is logically not possible. In JAGS this generates a message about "nodes inconsistent with parents".
I attached a simple example that demonstrated the issue.

Two other things to note:
1. In JAGS this situation crashes JAGS, but in NIMBLE it seems to move past the inconsistency, find the right values for z, and produce results that seem reasonable. So maybe it isn't cause for concern.
2. I don't remember this happening previously. Yesterday I (needlessly) ran the code suggested in Perry's post from yesterday, so I wonder if that could be relevant. I don't think so, because I tried my script on another computer with NIMBLE 0.7.0, and the behavior was the same. My version of NIMBLE is 0.7.1, and R is 3.4.3.

Any thoughts?

Thanks,
Glenn Stauffer

Hi Nick, further thoughts here:

In general, NIMBLE can create a placeholder rclayton function (it
won't do anything but it will satisfy NIMBLE's need for it to exist).
However, it sounds like you may have an 'rclayton' existing in your
global environment (or in some package namespace). If that's the case,
NIMBLE will see that rclayton and is probably seeing that the
arguments to that rclayton are not the same as for the dclayton that
you are defining.

A couple options are (1) create your own rclayton (as Joe pointed out)
-- this could just be a placeholder that doesn't really do anything,
or (2) make sure there is no 'rclayton' that can be found in your R
session -- in that case NIMBLE will create the placeholder.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
I think we've gotten off-track of Nick's question, which was about the error message he's getting from registerDistributions.

I think the issue is in the call to registerDistributions.  I think it should be:

registerDistributions(list(
  dclayton  = list(BUGSdist = 'dclayton(x,mu1,mu2,phi1,phi2,theta)',

                   types    = c('value = double(2)',

                                'mu1 = double(0)', 'mu2 = double(0)',
                                'phi1 = double(0)', 'phi2 = double(0)',
                                'theta = double(0)')
  )))

What may be confusing is that "value" is the label for the random variable itself, which in the d function is called "x".

We often use integer instead of double for the log argument, but I think double should work.

Also, you shouldn't need to call registerDistributions yourself if you are going to use it in just a simple way.  If you just use dclayton in a model, it will automatically be registered in a default way.  The utility of registerDistributions comes into play if you need to support alternative parameterizations or other details.

Glad to see this copula use of nimble.  Let us know further questions.

-Perry

  run = function(x = double(1), mu = double(1),

    returnType(double(0))

    v<-pbeta(x[2],mu[2]*phi[2],(1-mu[2])*phi[2])

    else return(exp(logProb)) })

  run = function(n=integer(0), mu= double(1), phi = double(1), theta = double(0)){

    )

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew, a few thoughts here:

Q1: that use of nimbleRcall looks good. There is some overhead in
going back and forth from compiled Nimble code to R (in particular we
have to
make copies of inputs and outputs), so that might slow things down a
bunch in some circumstances. To some degree whether it matters
will depend on how intensive the computations within R are and how
long the Kronecker call takes relative to the other stuff you are
doing.
Regardless, starting with nimbleRcall is a good way to prototype things.

Q2: yes, dwish is fine and the rest of the model code looks fine as well.
We have a list of the distribution names for Nimble in Sec. 5.2.4 of
the manual in case anyone is wondering.
But they are essentially the same names as in WinBUGS/JAGS.

chol() returns the upper triangular factor. Good point about the
documentation - we don't seem to say that explicitly,
but we do what R's chol() does. I'll make a note to fix up the docs.

Q3: You can use %*% for matrix-vector multiplication, either in model
code or in the run code of a nimbleFunction.

One thing to watch out for is that the result is a matrix (albeit with
one column).

So if you want to then later treat it as a vector, you'd need to do
something like this in model code:
result[1:m] <- (X[1:m,1:m] %*% y[1:m])[,1]
or in run code you don't need the indexing, but still need to do this
so that result is 1-d not 2-d:
result <- (X%*%y)[,1]
More discussion on this situation for nimbleFunction code is in Sec
11.3.2.5 of the manual.

-chris

messages.subject: Re: specifying inits in runMCMC
messages.body_plain:
Glenn, I'm sorry for the short delay on this, but it took us a while to track down exactly what was going on here.  For better or for worse, this had nothing to do with the MCMC, nor with the runMCMC function and it's handling of initial values which are provided as an argument.

Your example brought to light yet another "corner case" in terms of model initialization, the process in which nimble "inspects" model objects to make sure they are "fully initialized" -- that is, all nodes contain valid values, which are consistent with the rest of the model, and all model log-densities have been calculated and reflect the current values of stochastic nodes in the model.

Anyway, your example gave rise to a situation where intermediate deterministic nodes in the model (in your case, the pz[i]) were not having their values updated in the correct (topological) order, during the course of model initialization.  Thus, nimble was reporting that the values of the stochastic dependents (y[i]) were invalid, as a result of the "parent" deterministic probability nodes (pz[i]) not being calculated at the correct time.... if that makes sense.

The final thing I should say, is that this "model initialization" routine takes place at the beginning of every call to runMCMC(), that is, before the MCMC begins operating.

We've fixed this problem in the development branch of nimble.  The fix will be included in our next major/minor release, but until then, you can install the development version directly from GitHub, using:

devtools::install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble")

Please give it a go, and let us know if this clears up your problem.

And make sure to keep in touch with any further questions or problems that you have.

Cheers!
Daniel
for the NIMBLE development team

all but some very unusual situations) while the model initialization
reported something unusual,
by the end of the model initialization, everything was as it should

initialization
ended up with the correct initial values before the MCMC started,
despite temporarily doing some calculations with incorrect initial
values.

version the warning will disappear but the MCMC output should be
identical
to what you have already gotten.

And even in the unusual corner cases where the model initialization
was done "incorrectly", the MCMC output would still be valid, albeit
from
different starting values than planned.

Chris

Hi Andrew, a few thoughts here:

Q1: that use of nimbleRcall looks good. There is some overhead in going back and forth from compiled Nimble code to R (in particular we have to make copies of inputs and outputs), so that might slow things down a bunch in some circumstances. To some degree whether it matters will depend on how intensive the computations within R are and how long the Kronecker call takes relative to the other stuff you are doing.
Regardless, starting with nimbleRcall is a good way to prototype things.

Q2: yes, dwish is fine and the rest of the model code looks fine as well.
We have a list of the distribution names for Nimble in Sec. 5.2.4 of the manual in case anyone is wondering.
But they are essentially the same names as in WinBUGS/JAGS.

chol() returns the upper triangular factor. Good point about the documentation - we don't seem to say that explicitly, but we do what R's chol() does. I'll make a note to fix up the docs.

Q3: You can use %*% for matrix-vector multiplication, either in model code or in the run code of a nimbleFunction.

One thing to watch out for is that the result is a matrix (albeit with one column).

So if you want to then later treat it as a vector, you'd need to do something like this in model code:
result[1:m] <- (X[1:m,1:m] %*% y[1:m])[,1] or in run code you don't need the indexing, but still need to do this so that result is 1-d not 2-d:
result <- (X%*%y)[,1]
More discussion on this situation for nimbleFunction code is in Sec
11.3.2.5 of the manual.

-chris

messages.subject: notice of bug fix for dCRP users
messages.subject_clean: notice of bug fix for dCRP users
messages.body_plain:
Dear nimble-users members,

For those of you who are using the dCRP distribution in NIMBLE for
Bayesian non-parametric functionality, we've fixed a bug in version
0.7.0 that we wanted to make potentially-affected users aware of.

The bug was introduced in version 0.7.0 of NIMBLE (our most recent
version, released a few
weeks ago) during our efforts to improve efficiency of MCMC sampling
for BNP models. It causes incorrect MCMC sampling when using the dCRP
distribution in non-conjugate situations (i.e., where the base measure
and the mixture kernel are _not_ conjugate). For those of you who have
been using the dCRP distribution we ask that you update your version
of NIMBLE off our development version and rerun any MCMCs you've run.

To get the fix, please install NIMBLE from Github:

devtools::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble/packages/nimble@hotfix_bnp_update')

For those of you who are Windows users, you may need to do the
installation with administrative privileges. We've also heard a report
from a user that using the argument "force = TRUE" in the call to
install_github may help if you encounter an installation issue.

We'll also be including this fix in version 0.7.1 which should be
released in 2-3 weeks.

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team
